title: Trade off the piece doing the damage
outcomes: Names the most dangerous attacking piece and the exchange that removes it
Checks that an exchange removes an attacker the opponent cannot easily replace
Tells an exchange that fails, and a position that needs no exchange

steps.text:
When you are under attack, one **exchange** can do more than any quiet defensive move: it takes away the attacker's most dangerous piece.
Ask two questions. Which enemy piece is doing the damage? Which of my pieces can trade for it?
The rest of the lesson is about when this works and when it does not.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's knight and queen are aimed at the white king and queen.

line.say: The knight takes the knight on f4, the piece that attacks the queen on e2.
Black recaptures with the queen. One pair of knights is off the board.
White has traded off the knight that was aimed at the king and queen.

claims.statement: Nxf4 is the engine's first choice.
If White passes, Black has a forced win of material or mate.
The knight on f4 attacks the queen on e2 and the pawn on g2.
Ignoring the knight with g3 is at least two pawns worse.

steps.text:
**What to check.** An exchange helps when it removes an attacker the opponent cannot easily replace. Before you trade, ask: is a second attacker ready to take its place?
Then ask the reverse question: which of my pieces guards my king, and does this trade take it away?
**Rule of thumb:** fewer pieces usually help the defender, but only when the trade takes away the piece doing the damage.

steps.title: Same attack, one change
steps.prompt: In each position White is to move. Predict whether the exchange on f4 answers the attack, then check.
Which part was hardest: spotting the most dangerous attacker, checking whether the exchange removed it for good, or noticing that no exchange was needed?
